records.abstract: Barbara M. Altman, a Sociologist with a Ph.D. from the University of Maryland, is currently a Special Assistant on Disability Statistics at the National Center for Health Statistics and an Adjunct Associate Professor at the University of Maryland, College Park. Her previous position was Senior Research Fellow with the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality. She is a past president of the Society for Disability Studies and served on the founding Board of Directors of that organization. Her disability research interests focus in three areas: operationalization of disability definitions/measures in survey data; access to, financing and utilization of health care services by persons with disabilities, particularly working age persons and women with disabilities; and disability among minority groups. She is the author of a number of articles and book chapters on disability topics, and has served as editor of special issues of Disability Studies Quarterly and Journal of Disability Policy Studies. She is co-editor of this series Research in Social Science and Disability.Deborah J. Anderson, Ph.D., has conducted policy research in the area of Aging and Developmental Disabilities at the University of Minnesota since 1985. Her studies have included analyses of the health status, health conditions and health-related limitations and needs of older adults with mental retardation living in a variety of residential settings as well as in their own homes. These studies have included a longitudinal study of a 10% sample of older adults living in residential facilities licensed by developmental disabilities agencies, the National Nursing Home Survey of 1985, the National Medical Expenditure Survey of 1987, and the National Health Interview Disability Supplement (NHIS-D) of 1994–1995. She has also studied careproviders of older adults with mental retardation, innovative programs serving aging adults with developmental disabilities/mental retardation, and state agencies’ preparation for serving adults with mental retardation as they aged. Most of this research has been conducted as part of the NIDRR-funded RRTC on Aging and Developmental Disabilities. Dr. Anderson is also an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychology at St. Olaf College in Northfield, MN.Lynda L. Anderson, M.A., M.P.H., is a Resource Manager at No Place like Home in Robbinsdale, Minnesota. Ms. Anderson earned a Master of Arts degree in Human Service Administration and a Master of Public Health degree in Community Health. Ms. Anderson is a doctoral candidate in Work, Community and Family Education at the University of Minnesota. She has more than eighteen years of experience working with people with disabilities as a Direct Support Professional, Program Director, and Researcher. She has participated in NHIS-D analysis activities for the last five years.Sharon N. Barnartt, Ph.D., is Professor of Sociology at Gallaudet University. She has co-authored two books: Deaf President Now: The 1988 Revolution at Gallaudet University (1995) and Contentious Politics in the Disability and Deaf Communities (2001). She has also presented papers and published widely in the areas of socio-economic status and disability/deafness, legal and disability policy issues, and social movements in the deaf and disability communities. She is a former president of the Society for Disability Studies, co-editor of Research in Social Science and Disability and on the editorial board of Journal of Disability Policy Studies.Phillip W. Beatty, M.A., is a Senior Research Associate at the National Rehabilitation Hospital Center for Health & Disability Research in Washington, DC. His recent research focuses on predictors of access to health services among adults with disabilities. Mr. Beatty is also conducting research to determine the ways in which functional outcomes information is being used by stakeholders in the medical rehabilitation industry.Edward Brann, M.D., M.P.H., is Acting Director of the Division of Human Development and Disability, National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The division conducts a number of research and program activities for people with disabilities.Hong Chen, M.S., is an Economist in RTI International’s Division of Health Economics Research. His work focuses primarily on the analysis of large claims and survey databases, with an emphasis on diabetes prevention, substance abuse, and competitive bidding for durable medical equipment.Lisa J. Colpe, Ph.D., M.P.H., is a Clinical Epidemiologist Specializing in Survey Design and Research. At the time the work on this chapter was done, she was an Epidemiology Training Program Fellow in the Division of Health Interview Statistics, National Center for Health Statistics.Roger B. Davis, Sc.D., is Associate Professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School and Associate Professor of Biostatistics at the Harvard School of Public Health. Dr. Davis has overseen the statistical design of numerous clinical trials, especially involving cancer and AIDS therapies. An expert in survival analysis, he also participates in health services research and clinical epidemiology studies with colleagues at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, where he serves as Biostatistician in the Division of General Medicine and Primary Care.John Drabek, is an Economist in Office of Disability, Aging, and Long-Term Care Policy in the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. He received his B.A. in Economics from Northwestern University, and his Ph.D. in Economics from the University of California, Santa Barbara. Prior to joining the federal government, he performed research at the University of Southern California, and at the University of California, Los Angeles.Laura J. Dunlap, M.A., is a Health Economist in RTI International’s Center for Interdisciplinary Substance Abuse Research. Since joining RTI in 1994, she has worked on studies analyzing the costs and benefits of substance abuse treatment, the effect of treatment services on post-treatment outcomes, and the costs and cost-effectiveness of public health and treatment interventions aimed at special populations such as drug users and low-income women.Holly J. Fedeyko is a former employee of the Disability and Health Branch, CDC in Atlanta, Georgia. While at the CDC she focused her efforts on Research in disability issues as related to questions from the National Health Interview Survey. She received her M.P.H. in Epidemiology and Environmental Health from Emory and her B.S. in Biology from McGill. Goldscheider, University Professor and Professor of Sociology, began her Brown career in 1974. Goldscheider pioneered research on the single-person household, and on home leaving and return to the nest of young adults, and has examined issues of labor force and family decisions of 20th century American women. She is an expert on family structure and relationships, fertility, parenthood, household economy, and marriage. Grosse, Ph.D., is a Health Economist at the National Center for Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Hendershot, Ph.D., is a Consultant on Disability and Health Statistics. He had a lead role in promoting, designing, and analyzing the National Health Interview Survey on Disability. He is the author of many published statistical reports on disability and other health-related topics.Dennis P. Hogan, Professor of Sociology, joined the Population Studies and Training Center at Brown University in 1995. He received a Ph.D. in Sociology from the University of Wisconsin-Madison in 1976. He has taught at both the University of Chicago, where he acted as associate director of the Population Research Center, and Pennsylvania State University, where he served as director of the Population Research Institute. In 1997, Hogan was named to an endowed professorship as the Robert E. Turner Distinguished Professor of Population Studies. Some of his research interests include the interrelationships of the family lives of individuals and their social environments, the measurement of disability, family consequences of disability, and the transition to adulthood. Hogan’s current research focuses on child disability. He is the principal investigator on grants supporting this program from the National Institute for Child Health and Human Development, the National Center for Medical Rehabilitation Research, the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation, the Federal Interagency Forum on Child and Family Statistics Subcommittee on Disability and the Spencer Foundation.Ghada al Homsi, M.S., is an Economist in RTI International’s Center for Interdisciplinary Substance Abuse Research. Her work focuses on the analysis of large surveys and the design and maintenance of databases of program costs.Amanda A. Honeycutt, Ph.D., is an Economist in RTI International’s Division of Health Economics Research. Since joining RTI in 1998, she has led a number of studies on the cost-of-illness, the cost of intervention programs, and the cost-effectiveness of prevention and treatment interventions that focus primarily on diabetes, HIV/AIDS prevention, and children’s health, disability, and development.Peter C. Hunt, M.P.H., was an Association of Schools of Public Health Fellow in the Division of Health Interview Statistics, National Center for Health Statistics, at the time work on this chapter was done. He subsequently served as a Special Assistant to the Director of the National Institute of Disability and Rehabilitation Research. He is currently a Research Associate at the University of Pittsburgh Model Center on Spinal Cord Injury.Lisa I. Iezzoni, M.D., M.Sc., is Professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School and Co-Director of Research in the Division of General Medicine and Primary Care, Department of Medicine, at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston. Her primary research interest is risk adjustment for assessing health care quality and improving the fairness of payments. A 1996 recipient of The Robert Wood Johnson Foundation Investigator Award in Health Policy Research, she also studies health policy issues relating to mobility impairments. Dr. Iezzoni is a member of the Institute of Medicine.Gwyn C. Jones, Ph.D., M.S.W., M.Ed., is a Senior Research Associate at the National Rehabilitation Hospital Center for Health & Disability Research in Washington, DC. She is a former ATPM/CDC Fellow and current grantee. Her research and publications have focused on health risks, chronic conditions, and use of preventive services among working-age adults with disabilities, prescription drug use among non-elderly adults with disabilities, and rural Medicaid managed care for adults with disabilities.Judith D. Kasper, Ph.D., is a Professor in the Department of Health Policy and Management, and a Senior Research Associate in the Center for Health Services Research, at The Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Her research interests include health policy in long-term care, aging and disability, access to health care for vulnerable populations, and the development and application of data sources for health policy and health services research. Dr. Kasper holds a Ph.D. in sociology from the University of Chicago.K. Charlie Lakin, Ph.D., is the Director of the Research and Training Center on Community Living at the University of Minnesota. Mr. Lakin has had extensive experience in gathering, analyzing, and using statistics from many primary and secondary data sources with the products of this work included in more than 200 publications in developmental disabilities and related services. Mr. Lakin was a member of the six-person external technical advisory panel on the instrumentation for the Disability Supplement. Mr. Lakin serves as Associate Editor of Mental Retardation, and consulting editor of The Journal of the Association for Persons with Severe Handicaps (JASH), the Journal on Intellectual and Developmental Disability and Social Science and Disability.Sheryl A. Larson, Ph.D., is a Research Associate at the Research and Training Center on Community Living at the University of Minnesota. She earned her Ph.D. in Educational Psychology from the University of Minnesota. She has 20 years of experience in services to persons with DD as a residential counselor, behavior analyst, social worker, and program evaluator and has worked for the RTC for the last 14 years. Ms. Larson was the Co-Principal Investigator for a two-year NIDRR Field Initiated Project which used the National Health Interview Survey Disability Supplement to examine the characteristics and service needs of persons with intellectual or developmental disabilities. She directed a supplement to the Research and Training Center on Community Living’s core grant that funded an international user’s conference in June 2000 for researchers analyzing NHIS-D topics. She has co-authored several papers using NHIS-D data. Dr. Larson has also co-authored several books, book chapters, journal articles and technical reports on workforce development issues, residential services, and community integration for persons with developmental disabilities and is a consulting editor of Mental Retardation.Donald J. Lollar, Ed.D., Senior Research Scientist, Division for Human Development and Disability, National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in Atlanta. His advanced degrees are from Indiana University, and his most recent writings include co-editing an Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation supplement on the Science of Disability Outcomes, and articles for the 2003 Annual Review of Public Health and 2002 Public Health Reports outlining public health strategies to improve the health and well-being of people with disabilities. He has spent the past seven years developing public health science and programs to improve the health of people with disabilities, prevent secondary conditions, and increase participation in society. He currently serves as the co-lead of the Healthy People 2010 workgroup on Disability and Secondary Conditions (Chap. 6 of HP 2010). Dr. Lollar began involvement with the WHO classification ICIDH in 1994 while still in private practice, assessing potential utility of ICIDH-2 for clinical records. He is currently a part of the team to adapt the ICF to improve its utility for children and youth.Pamela Loprest is a Labor Economist and Senior Research Associate at the Urban Institute. Her research focuses on low-wage labor markets and how government policies can help to reduce and remove barriers to work among disadvantaged populations. Dr. Loprest has a Ph.D. in Economics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and has been at the Urban Institute since 1991.Elaine Maag is a Research Associate in the Urban Institute’s Income and Benefits Policy Center. Her research focuses on policies affecting youth with disabilities and employment opportunities for adults. She also conducts research on how tax policy affects low-income families. Ms. Maag holds an M.S. in Public Policy from the University of Rochester.Jennifer M. Park is a Post-Doctoral Fellow at the Harvard Graduate School of Education. Her current research is funded by a grant she holds from the American Education Research Association to examine cognitive development among first grade youth with and without emotional impairment. Her dissertation explored cognitive growth among kindergarteners with and without perceptual impairment. Dr. Park holds a Ph.D. in Sociology from Brown University, where her research examined the diverse effects of child disability on family outcomes.Elizabeth K. Rasch, M.S., P.T., is an Associate Service Fellow at the National Center for Health Statistics, CDC, working in the area of disability statistics. Her research interests include the health of persons with disabilities, factors that contribute to disability, as well as the use of and access to healthcare services by persons with disabilities. She has been actively involved in research since 1985 and has published articles and book chapters on topics related to disability and rehabilitation.Anne W. Riley, is an Associate Professor in the Department of Health Policy and Management, in the division of Health Services Research, at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Dr. Riley has expertise in the assessment of mental health and health, especially of children and adolescents, methods development, and evaluation systems for monitoring the outcomes of care for youth.Diana E. Schendel, Ph.D., is a Lead Health Scientist at the National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Verbrugge, Ph.D., M.P.H., is Distinguished Senior Research Scientist in the Institute of Gerontology at the University of Michigan. Witt, Ph.D., M.P.H., is an Assistant Professor of Medicine in the Division of General Internal Medicine and Center for Healthcare Studies at the Northwestern University, Feinberg School of Medicine. She holds a Ph.D. in health services research and a M.P.H. from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and a B.A. in women’s studies and law from Hampshire College.Li-shou Yang, Ph.D., is Research Investigator in the Institute for Social Research at the University of Michigan. records.title: Two Million Black Americans Born Prior to Emancipation in the 1900 U.S. Census
records.norm_title: two million black americans born prior to emancipation in the 1900 u s census
records.venue: Journal of Slavery and Data Preservation
records.authors: Ras Michael Brown; Britton Davis; Joseph Price; Elizabeth West
records.abstract: Dataset CreatorsFamilySearch InternationalJoseph Price, Brigham Young UniversityTracing people from the era of enslavement into the generations that followed emancipation presents exceptional challenges to descendants and researchers. Chief among these is the lack of key demographic data, which inhibits the creation of detailed snapshots and diachronic perspectives on most individuals and communities impacted by slavery and its aftermath. Even when we can find names and personal details from specific collections and aggregate information in discrete datasets, linking individual people and larger groups between multiple sources remains difficult. This limitation complicates efforts to trace individuals and identify connections to kin and community over time, and precludes any large-scale attempt to assess the whole population of formerly enslaved people in the decades after emancipation. A potential solution lies in creating a comprehensive baseline dataset that provides the broadest range of demographic information for Black Americans born at or before general emancipation in 1865.1 In addition to providing comprehensive demographic data suitable for linking to other collections, such a dataset would establish kinship and community networks of foundational knowledge essential for unearthing earlier generations to reconstruct relationships between formerly enslaved people, their immediate kin, their descendants, and the communities in which they lived. This dataset, created based on FamilySearch International’s index of the 1900 U.S. Census, provides the broadest possible baseline necessary for these multiple levels of inquiry available to date.The dataset supplies access to significant information documented for the first time in a federal census and available for the first time in a census-based dataset. In each U.S. census following emancipation, the federal government documented increasing details about the millions of women, men, and children who had been enslaved. The initial post-emancipation census in 1870 enumerated 4.1 million Black Americans born prior to 1866, capturing their full name, age, household members, and state of birth. As much insight as this historic census provided, it lacked important details documented three decades later. The 1900 U.S. Census represents the earliest surviving manuscript collection that included birth month and year for fully named individuals, along with gender, civil status (single, married, widowed), years married, the relationship to the head of the household, the numbers of children (both total and living children for each mother), occupation, and homeownership, along with geographic life markers, such as places of birth and current census district. Our dataset features key variables directly from the 1900 U.S. Census such as birth month and year, gender, state of birth, and the census district in which each individual was enumerated. Most importantly, the dataset includes the names of the 2,080,169 Black Americans born before 1866 and enumerated among the more than 8 million in the 1900 census. Until now, no census-based dataset focused on formerly enslaved and free Black people has made these names publicly available.2Before turning to examples of possible applications of the dataset, it is essential to recognize that the 1900 U.S. Census was conducted in the midst of an era later coined by historian Rayford W. Logan as “The Nadir” in the social and political status of Black Americans after emancipation.3 White people throughout the South used legal and economic weapons along with physical violence to disenfranchise and impoverish Black citizens in a system based on racial segregation and oppression. Many of the gains in the decades following emancipation had been undone, though Black Americans of all social classes throughout the nation remained ardent activists.4 Notably, starting in the decade before the 1900 U.S. Census, many formerly enslaved people identified themselves as “ex-slaves,” formed “ex-slave” associations, and petitioned the US government for pensions as recompense for the work and disabilities they experienced in slavery.5 Predictably, their claims were rejected. The world of formerly enslaved people and their free-born descendants in 1900 grew increasingly unstable and dangerous. These circumstances set the stage for significant developments, most remarkably the beginning of the Great Migration, which in subsequent decades would see the migration of millions of Black Americans out of the South.6 Additionally, data culled from the 1900 U.S. Census formed an early statistical basis for economic and social analyses shaped by emerging forms of scientific racism. At the same time, Black scholars, particularly W. E. Burghardt DuBois, employed the 1900 U.S. Census to develop social scientific knowledge for the benefit of African Americans.7 These diametrically opposed purposes driven by the same source of data from the 1900 U.S. Census should encourage users of our dataset to operate in full awareness of the ethics of care needed for framing research questions and presenting arguments based on all forms of Black data.8Our dataset provides a large sample of those with a high likelihood of being formerly enslaved. We do not pretend to know which ones were in the enslaved population, but given about 90 percent were, this dataset will be a starting place for research in the area and be useful for broad level claims. Due to a spike in recording birth year in 1865 (age-heaping was common practice), errors in census enumeration, and the fact that approximately 11 percent of Black Americans in 1865 were born free, we plead caution in labeling any individual as formerly enslaved without further evidence or linkage.An analysis of Black Americans in the state of Mississippi illustrates the layered research potential of the “Two Million Black Americans Born Prior to Emancipation in the 1900 U.S. Census” dataset. In 1900, the 907,630 Black residents of Mississippi comprised 58.5 percent of all inhabitants (the highest proportion in any state) and the second-highest population of Black descendants living in any state (Georgia being first with 1,034,813 Black residents). Among these residents, 198,451 (22 percent) were old enough to have been enslaved, very few of whom would have been among the extremely small free Black community in the state before the Civil War. The dataset allows researchers to focus on county and census district levels to find, for example, that 5,692 (22 percent) of Black Americans enumerated in Noxubee County are likely formerly enslaved people, with 1,035 of these women (#529) and men (#506) living in “Beat 4” (“Beat” being the census district label used in Mississippi) of the county. Once researchers filter for these individuals, they can follow Family Tree Person ID links to view all variables recorded in the manuscript census document and pursue specific topics of interest. Researchers concerned with extent of land ownership among formerly enslaved people, for example, can use the dataset results to identify relevant individuals and then access each of the 1,035 links to discover who among them owned their homes (and likely their own farmland) and who rented (and likely farmed as sharecroppers). Additionally, the links to manuscript sources permit researchers to examine households and kin relationships, raising questions such as: how many formerly enslaved women in Beat 4 of Noxubee County lived as widows in multigenerational households? How many formerly enslaved couples married before emancipation? Although the dataset cannot answer these particular questions, it can help identify and link to individuals whose manuscript census information can then be accessed and aggregated to create new datasets designed by researchers.The “Two Million Black Americans Born Prior to Emancipation in the 1900 U.S. Census” dataset can sort variables to provide definitive answers to specific questions, such as how many of the formerly enslaved residents of Noxubee County’s Beat 4 had been born in states other than Mississippi. Exploration into this question can shed significant light on how the forced migration of Black Americans across the antebellum South shaped Black sensibilities of place, home, and belonging before the Great Migration of the 20th Century. Given Mississippi’s brief pre-Civil War history as a territory and state in the United States combined with its primary role as a colony for plantation slavery, the displacement of people from other states to Mississippi was central to the formation of enslaved families and communities leading up to the Civil War and Emancipation. In Beat 4, 39 percent (399) of formerly enslaved people recorded in 1900 were born outside Mississippi, including in Alabama, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia, Washington, D.C., and Georgia. Among those from Georgia was Shad (misspelled “Shed”) Cistrunk born in 1848, whose Family Tree Person ID link shows that he lived with his wife Susan and daughter Sophia, both born in Mississippi. Shadrick (his full first name) Cistrunk presents a special use of the dataset for researchers starting with individual information and wanting to search at a larger level. In her book Finding Francis, Elizabeth West tells the family story of the change in the spelling of her ancestors’ surname during Reconstruction. The story holds that Shadrick and his brothers changed the spelling of their name from “Sistrunk” to “Cistrunk” to distinguish their family from white Sistrunks in their county whose progenitors once enslaved them and their mother, Francis. Their uncommon surname has enabled West to use the dataset to confirm her family’s story, as the only Cistrunks in Noxubee County, Mississippi, were kin of the sons of Francis. All the formerly enslaved people named Sistrunk lived in other states, including Alabama and South Carolina.9The “birthplace” variable in the dataset can be utilized to reveal another dimension of the movements of Black Americans, this time after emancipation. Though the “Great Migration” had not yet commenced, by the close of the nineteenth century, Black movement north and westward had already begun via established routes from the South, where nearly 90 percent of Black Americans still lived in 1900. The 1900 census reveals earlier migrations of many Blacks from the South in the aftermath of the Civil War. Of the 31,838 Black Americans in Chicago (Cook County, IL) in 1900, 9,631 (3.6 percent) had been born and enslaved in Mississippi. Following the Family Tree Person ID of Jane Ellis, born in Mississippi in August of 1845, reveals important details from the census. She lived with her husband, George (born in Tennessee), and their daughter Ella Walker, and granddaughter Ebbie (both born in Illinois). Another Family Tree Person ID links to the manuscript image that shows Junius Holman, born in 1839 in Mississippi, residing with his wife, Nancy (born in Virginia), and their grandson Francis (born in Illinois). Though not included in the dataset, the geographical markers for the birthplace of parents appeared in the 1900 census and indicates that Junius’s mother and father had been born in Virginia. The combination of the dataset with its links to other sources in Family Tree allows researchers to explore various levels of the forced and voluntary movements Black Americans experienced throughout the nineteenth century.These layers of demographic information allow researchers to analyze data beyond individual profile mapping made possible through FamilySearch, Ancestry, MyHeritage, or FindMyPast, while still taking advantage of the extensive genealogical resources accessible through FamilySearch. In addition to census information, we include a 7-digit Family Tree Person ID (PID) for 1,766,103 individuals in the dataset to enable users to follow any PID link to a Family Tree “ancestors page” without needing a FamilySearch login. Profiles on the Family Tree are created and updated by individuals doing family history research. In their research, patrons of FamilySearch add in data on birth dates, death dates, and places, and support these conclusions by attaching historical records as sources. These ancestor pages include source images from the 1900 U.S. Census (and occasionally other historical records), records documenting other members of the principal’s family, and a timeline of significant events in the lives of each principal and often their relatives (birth, marriage, birth of children, death, etc.). Additionally, they provide broad discussions of historical contexts for relevant world events.If users create a free FamilySearch account, they can also enter their own family tree data and potentially determine if and how they are related to these formerly enslaved and free individuals. The profiles on the Family Tree are dynamic and change over time as individuals add or edit information on the profile. We also encourage academic and family researchers to compare the conclusions on the Family Tree with other resources in order to arrive at the level of certainty required to draw probable conclusions. Family Tree provides the following resources for non-logged-in user access to: source images from the 1900 U.S. Census and occasionally other historical records;records documenting other members of the principal’s family;historical context to world events; anda timeline of events from the lives of each principal and, in many cases, their family members (birth, marriage, birth of children, death, etc.).The crowdsourcing capabilities of Family Tree have been instrumental to the development of multiple record-linking projects and will enable the continued enhancement of the “2 Million Black Americans Born Prior to Emancipation in the 1900 US Census” dataset as a portal to deeper research possibilities.10 For descendants especially, access to Family Tree with free FamilySearch accounts allows users to explore their connections to formerly enslaved individuals and input their own genealogical information, rendering Family Tree even more helpful for descendants hoping to find and create kinship ties. These contributions by descendants in turn strengthen the scholarly research that integrates the Family Tree into its methodology, enriching our understanding of the lives of formerly enslaved and free Black people and their families.2008-2011EnglishUnited States1900Census'United States Census, 1900.' FamilySearch. https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/collection/1325221. Citing NARA microfilm publication T623. Washington, D.C.: National Archives and Records Administration, n.d.The 1900 U.S. Census includes approximately 76,200,00 individuals. Several years ago, FamilySearch acquired licensed images of this collection from the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA).As a result of the efforts of many thousands of indexing volunteers, FamilySearch completed the full index of this collection. The following fields were included: Name, Sex, Age, Birth Date, Birthplace, Marital Status, Race, Number of Living Children, Number of Children, Relationship to Head of Household, Father's Birthplace, Mother's Birthplace, Event Type, Event Date, Event Place, Household Identifier, Line Number, Sheet Letter, Sheet Number, Affiliate Publication Number, Affiliate Number.Approximately 9 million individuals are identified in the 1900 census as Black Americans (¼ Black, ½ Black, Black, Colored, Mulatto, Negro, etc.). With this race information, birth month, year, and age, we restricted this published dataset to include only individuals born before emancipation (prior to January 1, 1866, shortly after the 13th Amendment was ratified on December 6, 1865). Using these filtering methods, 89 percent of these 2,080,169 Black individuals were identified as very likely once enslaved. Approximately 11 percent were free Black Americans.11 The full index provides access to the original census page digital image and family relationships as documented in the census.(e.g. https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:M9XS-9RB/?cid=partner-enslaved-org).In Fig. 1 below, we create a heatmap that provides the counts of the number of individuals in our sample based on their state of residence in the 1900 Census.In Fig. 2 below, we create a similar heat map but this time provide the number of people in our sample based on the birth state reported in the Census record.Table 1 below displays a transition matrix that illustrates the probabilities of individuals transitioning from their birth state to their current residence state. This matrix is constructed with each row representing the state of birth and each column corresponding to the current residence state in 1900.Fig. 3 below shows a histogram displaying the density of birth years for the two million Black Americans born prior to emancipation in the 1900 census, overlaid by recorded gender. The spikes in the graph occur mostly on the even number such as 1850, 1855, etc. and can be explained by a common pattern in census records of “age heaping,” or rounding to nearby focus numbers when reporting age.In addition to the information that is provided in the 1900 Census record, we have also gathered data on the profiles of these individuals on the Family Tree. Currently, 84 percent of the individuals in our dataset have a Family Tree profile. Many of these profiles have been created using a combination of automated tools developed by the BYU Record Linking Lab and the efforts of thousands of volunteers who have created or connected profiles to the 1900 Census.For the individuals in our dataset who have a connection to a profile on the Family Tree, we have provided a FamilySearch Person ID (PID). PID links enable tracking of individuals throughout their lifespan by connecting them to a global community-created tree. As discussed above, information on family members, marriage records, death records, birth records, and other census records could be found on a profile.Table 2 below displays the percentage of our sample that has a PID. The table also specifies what share of individuals in the dataset have a death date, which can be useful when examining which census records we would expect to find the person in. Since Family Tree profiles are crowdsourced, the fraction of individuals in this sample that have death dates will increase as individuals attach additional sources to the profiles like death certificates and cemetery records.The rows in Table 2 are divided based on the relationship to the head of the household according to the 1900 Census. Because Family Tree is designed to document and expand family relationships, the primary focus of the work that we did with volunteers and automated tools, which used the FamilySearch API and its write function to directly attach census information, was to add households with two or more related individuals to the Family Tree. As a result, the FamilySearch profile coverage rates for individuals who were a head, wife, son, or daughter are now all above 90 percent, whereas other groups can have much lower rates of coverage on the Family Tree.June 2025Dataset Repository: Harvard Dataverse, https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/JSHPJTProject Website: https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/collection/1325221FamilySearch InternationalChurch of Jesus Christ of Latter-day SaintsBYU Record Linking Lab

records.title: Home Trap
records.norm_title: home trap
records.abstract: It's a beautiful snare, the myth of a home, and I step into the noosed loop every time.The knot tightens when I try to move away; the cord whips me up into the trees, swinging over twelve generations. I can catch a glimpse of a ship docked off Cape Cod and hear a newborn cry rising over the din of sixty-some Pilgrims crammed inside the wooden walls of the Mayflower's hull. I can twist to pivot as 400 miles north, another infant shrieks, affronted at her removal from a warm womb into the frigid Laurentian winter seeping through cracks in the barely habitable shelter of L'Habitation.It is 1620, and Peregrine White and Hélène Desportes are newborn flags shoved into the loam of North America, the original anchor babies. But they are also helixes, roots coiling beneath the soil for nearly four centuries, twisting until they taper and touch to make me, a girl who grows up choked by her certainty that she has never had a home.Hélène Desportes \ ill-enn DEPORT \ (n.): Torch of the Doors.Peregrine White \ PAIR-a-grin white \ (n.): a White foreigner.These are my forebears, these foreigners burning down the doors to get inside: two immigrant children recorded in the baby calendars of two nations as the First White Child Born on their land-grabs of North America. The Pilgrims and French habitants didn't crown Peregrine and Hélène as the First Child Born—the evidence that they were both squatting on centuries of native-occupied land was everywhere. But white history marks trespasses as beginnings, and so Peregrine's and Hélène's names were documented as the heralds of their foundling fatherlands, tent stakes of invasion, fastening their families to some sort of claim on the future.Hélène begot Agnès begot Agnès begot Barthélemy begot Marie-Catherine begot Marie-Hypolite begot Jean-Baptiste begot John Baptist begot Monroe begot Beulah begot Katrina begot me.Peregrine begot Sylvanus begot William begot Abner begot Charles begot Abner begot Ethan begot Abner begot Adeline begot Royal begot Lorraine begot David begot me.There was a graduate student and his young wife, clipping coupons in a West Lafayette apartment, six hundred miles away from the place they had, until recently, called home. The graduate student was teaching a summer class, maybe his wife was resting on the plastic lawn chaise they still used as indoor furniture four years after leaving the familiar frozen shores of Minnesota for a land-grant university on a Hoosier field. I would suggest the graduate student's wife was on the telephone with her mother, but that would have been an expensive long-distance call; she would have waited until she had something to share. Her body tightened and cramped in a rhythmic, unfamiliar pain. She was admitted into a sterile medical room at Home Hospital where she squatted on a birthing chair and bore her daughter, the first child in four generations to emerge somewhere other than home though paradoxically, of course, she was born at Home.That is not strictly true; my oldest cousin was born in England, where my uncle was temporarily stationed, but if I had said “the first child in four direct generations,” that specificity would hint at the shaping of a narrative, demanding recalibration while I am preoccupied with collecting errant facts. I know this: My cousin returned home to Minnesota before his first birthday. I know this as well: My cousin has spent the rest of his life within ten miles of the house where his mother and my mother were children, the house my great-grandfather built. But I know this best: My mother took me home less than ten times before that house was sold, yet I can still draw a map of every room.Peregrine White arrived in late November or early December of 1620, born aboard the Mayflower while it was anchored inside Cape Cod. Peregrine was actually the second child born to the Pilgrims, since Oceanus Hopkins arrived mid-voyage, but Oceanus's birth apparently did not matter to the historians. Perhaps that is because Peregrine was born with their new homeland in actual sight, born on the boat hovering right outside of the place that would become home. Peregrine's mother Susanna somehow kept her infant son alive through the winter they spent docked on the ship with the other Pilgrims, who sickened and died in droves. Peregrine White spent his first months on the water, never touching solid ground.I've played the Jamestown simulation game at my local history museum. I spun the wheel and received a snake bite, lost Morale points, escaped or succumbed to the catalog of catastrophes that befell the early colonists in America. I know half the Mayflower colony died during that first winter before they even tried to stake their claim onshore. What surprises me, still, is that this infant boy survived a winter that killed his father. How did Susanna make milk to nurse Peregrine? She must have snuggled Peregrine to her body at night to keep him warm, half-smothering him as the hammock swayed.Or maybe she didn't; I've seen online pictures of the woven-willow-shoot cradle the Pilgrim Hall Museum claims Peregrine used. Susanna had boarded the Mayflower when she was seven months pregnant—I can imagine her demanding they make room in the hold for the future bed of the First White Child to be Born in America. But I wonder if Oceanus Hopkins got to use Peregrine's cradle first. The Pilgrims were arriving on occupied land; I believe the cradle of Mayflower civilization was also pre-occupied.When Jacques Cartier landed at Stadacona, the home of the Laurentian Iroquois, which would be taken by the French and renamed Québec, the land was occupied. Kaniatarowanenneh—the river that would be renamed the St. Lawrence—was thickly lined with villages. Over seventy years later, Samuel de Champlain followed Cartier's maps to Stadacona to establish L'Habitation, but Champlain found no Iroquoian settlements along the river. Champlain claimed the indigenous people had “disappeared.” For five hundred years prior, the people had actually occupied and unoccupied their land, waves of movement and waves of reclamation lapping against the shores of Kaniatarowanenneh, but the French needed to believe the land was vacant. If it was vacant, it was available.But if you cut a small hole in a piece of paper and hold it over a map, watching the same land for two hundred years, migratory people will appear and disappear. It is easy to believe they have disappeared entirely if you do not lift up the paper to see they have only walked fifty miles south—out of view, not off the earth.Hélène Desportes was born onto that reoccupied territory of Stadacona in 1620, the streaming waters of Kaniatarowanenneh rinsing away the afterbirth of the First White Child Born on claimed Québec soil. Perhaps her mother understood the importance of her newborn daughter's position and sought to secure it—the baby's godmother was Hélène's namesake: Champlain's wife.Champlain drew a map of Plymouth Harbor in 1605, fifteen years before the Pilgrims set sail. The map detailed the thriving village of the Patuxet Wampanoag, home of Tisquantum. A white man kidnapped Tisquantum in 1614 and took him to Europe; when Tisquantum escaped and returned to Patuxet five years later, his village had been obliterated by white-borne plague. The only living Patuxet Wampanoag was Tisquantum, who was left to sift through the wreckage, to bury the bones, to cradle his memories of home.The first time the Pilgrims touched their New World was actually inside the curled tip of Cape Cod near modern-day Provincetown Harbor, not at “Plymouth Rock.” A small group of Pilgrims went ashore and, finding no one alive, raided the camp of the Nauset Wampanoag for scraps of corn. But when the remaining Nauset met the interloping Pilgrim party, the Nauset furiously chased them out. The Mayflower sailed across the bay and anchored outside Patuxet, the emptied land that would shortly be renamed Plymouth.Home is what you steal, home is what you guard, home is a lock and you're twisting the dial, fumbling to release the shackle. Or to engage it.I like trap metaphors. records.title: A Comment on Family Law in Israel, following Sovereignty and Religious Freedom: A Jewish History by Simon Rabinovitch
records.norm_title: a comment on family law in israel following sovereignty and religious freedom a jewish history by simon rabinovitch
records.abstract: In the third chapter of his book, titled Marriage, Divorce, and Jewish Exceptions, Rabinovitch provides a clear and compelling description of the anomalous situation of family law in Israel—the only jurisdiction in the world that has two State court systems, one civil and one religious,1 implementing a hybridity of civil and religious family law.2 While not referring to all significant relevant scholarship,3 Rabinovitch’s account of the content of Jewish family law and its discriminatory impact on women is likewise thorough and important.4 The third chapter’s contribution lies first in enlightening non-Israeli readers about the almost unbelievable socio-legal reality in which a state that defines itself as a democracy nevertheless does not allow civil marriage and divorce, and coerces its population to obey religious laws and courts. Indeed, this is one of the main ways in which the Jewish collective overrides individual basic rights in its modern nation-state. Second, this chapter is extremely timely, as the tension between the “democratic” and the “Jewish” components within the identity of the State of Israel5 seems more incompatible than ever before. In the chapter, Rabinovitch examines how Jewish family law has been accommodated, contested, or constrained by different state legal systems across a wide historical and geographic spectrum, through a gendered lens. Structured as a series of case studies, the chapter starts with the Russian Empire’s need to address the tension between converted male Jews’ interests in ignoring their Jewish marriage and the neglected Jewish spouse who cannot be released without a Get; It then turns to the Ottoman Empire’s Tanzimat reforms, which formalized separate religious court systems for each religious collective, and these reforms’ influence on the British Mandate in Palestine and the following contemporary State of Israel, creating a contradiction with the latter’s commitment to equality between the sexes; then followed by the Israeli Rabbinical Courts’ unusual international jurisdiction; the approach of U.S.’ legislation and civil courts toward religious documents and marriage contracts, which challenges the alleged separation between religion and State; and finally to the collective right of religious communities, including the Jewish one, to excommunicate members in democratic South Africa. This historical breadth of Rabinovitch’s analysis, spanning centuries and continents, enables illuminating comparisons across time and place regarding the tension between individual rights and the rights of Jews as a collective. Throughout the chapter, he illustrates this tension through detailed legal cases that highlight the consequences of religious legal authority operating under the commitment to religious law, within or alongside state jurisdiction and jurisprudence. By comparing all the case studies mentioned above, Rabinovitch shows that judicial decisions in cases involving conflicts between individual and communal rights are shaped less by a state’s formal stance on the separation of religion and state, and more by political and ideological considerations. In other words, courts do not consistently favor either individual autonomy or collective religious authority based on legal principles alone. Instead, their rulings tend to reflect whether the actions at stake align with or challenge the state’s broader view of its foundational values, national identity, or principles of justice. This main theme of the tension between collective and individual rights, which is echoed throughout the book as a whole, and particularly in the third chapter in the realm of Jewish family law, highlights Israel’s deep and unresolved conflict between women’s right to equality and dignity on the one hand, and the rights6 of the Jewish collective to preserve its religious traditions, cultural practices, and national identity, on the other hand. While we of course agree with Rabinovitch that there is a harsh conflict between women’s rights and religious-collective rights in Israel, we nevertheless wish to problematize the way it is framed by him on three levels: first, by questioning what is actually known about family law in action in Israel; second, by asking whether Israeli civil family courts are indeed more favorable to women than religious courts; and third, by further contesting the very notion of a unified “Jewish collective” in the Israeli context, whose rights are being protected. In the chapter’s conclusion, and based on a news article, Rabinovitch cites a case in which the: Jerusalem Rabbinical Court fined a woman NIS 100,000 for seeking a police restraining order against her ex-husband (who owed NIS 100,000 in child support payments and was harassing her) because their divorce agreement included a clause stating that neither party could use civil authorities without permission from the rabbinical court.7 We were not familiar with this case, which sounds outrageous indeed, and had assumed, based on our legal understanding, that it was unlikely that such a decision would withstand judicial review by the Great Rabbinical Court or the Supreme Court.8 In an attempt to learn about the case beyond the news report, and based on our assumption that there was probably an appeal, we searched for related court decisions. However, despite our efforts, we located none. Subsequently, we contacted the Center for Women’s Justice,9 which represented the woman in that case. The lawyer involved informed us that indeed an appeal had been submitted to the Great Rabbinical Court, but unexpectedly, and before the appeal was heard, the Regional Rabbinical Court issued a new ruling that effectively annulled its own previous decision.10 First, this outcome suggests that the situation may not be as dire as it appears in Rabinovitch’s account. Second, it also exemplifies a broader problem we wish to address here—the difficulty of truly knowing Israeli family law in action. Family law proceedings are common in Israeli Jewish society, hence relevant to a significant part of Israel’s population. For example, in 2023 alone, over 10,000 couples divorced, and more than 100,000 proceedings were filed in the Rabbinical courts.11 That same year, approximately 90,000 additional cases were filed in the Family Courts.12 Still, the Israeli judicial system has yet to develop a systematic mechanism for publishing rulings in this field. In fact, most judicial decisions related to family matters in civil and religious courts are unpublished, leaving most of the formal legal actions in this field in the dark, hidden from public view. The confidential nature of family law proceedings, which are held in Israel almost entirely behind closed doors,13 and the legitimate concern for protecting litigants’ privacy, necessitate the anonymization of judgments. However, in the absence of an institutionalized framework to ensure the routine and comprehensive publication of anonymized decisions, the body of rulings available to practitioners and scholars remains limited to those selectively published at the discretion of individual judges.14 This selective publication undermines the ability to assess whether the available rulings accurately reflect prevailing legal interpretations or broader judicial trends, and it hinders critical examination of individual judges’ concrete decisions. The lack of transparency and accountability is even greater in the religious courts, which publish their decisions only sporadically, if at all.15 Moreover, much of what takes place in the field of family law occurs in “the shadow of the law,” through off-the-record interactions in the courtroom that leave no written trace. While this is an important practice used by judges to advance compromises, it diminishes transparency and enhances the severely limited ability to comprehensively know what is actually going on in the area of family law.16 The issue of transparency and accountability in family law proceedings in Israel has drawn growing public and institutional attention in recent years. The first to challenge the situation was Professor Moussa Abu Ramadan, who petitioned the High Court of Justice over the barriers he experienced as a researcher of the Sharia Courts. The High Court of Justice dismissed the petition, stating that the general request for publication of rulings was moot due to existing practices since the 2001 amendment to the Religious Courts (Enforcement of Compliance and Procedure) Law, 5716–1956, which states that proceedings before the Sharia courts are to be held in closed hearings. Accordingly, their rulings may only be published under an ad hoc judicial decision and with identifying details redacted. It further held that the petitioner is not entitled to special access, emphasizing that rights such as academic freedom and transparency in the justice system are relative and may be limited in order to protect legitimate privacy interests.17 Next, a governmental committee was established, with the involvement of the first author, to look for ways to balance the public’s right to know what occurs behind judicially closed doors, with competing rights and interests, primarily privacy and security.18 This committee’s work was halted after two years, among other reasons, due to the establishment of another governmental committee, known as the Englard Committee, which was given a similar yet broader mandate. It took 13 years for this committee to publish a report, which recommends that, as a general rule, judicial decisions rendered in civil proceedings shall be published with identifying details omitted. However, the committee did not specifically address family law proceedings or the Family Courts and religious courts in its recommendations.19 During that long period, another petition was submitted to the Israeli High Court of Justice, demanding greater transparency in this legal field, this time in relation to the civil family courts.20 This petition resulted in a recommendation that each family court judge publish one decision per month.21 Like the petition of Abu Ramadan, this petition did not dramatically change matters on the ground.22 Recently, two legislative proposals to amend the Courts Bill were introduced in the Knesset, proposing that family courts be required to publish their decisions and rulings, with identifying details of the parties involved removed, within 21 days of the decision’s issuance.23 The fact that one proposal was brought by an MK from the coalition and the other by an MK from the opposition is interesting in light of the extreme and unprecedented political rift within the Knesset, and might enhance the chance for change in the field. If the law is changed, it will also apply to the Rabbinical Courts,24 and hence it will save the semi-detective work that was needed to explore what happened in the case mentioned by Rabinovitch, which we started with. Such a change could also be relevant to another example discussed by Rabinovitch, when he discusses civil courts’ apparent preference for the religious parent over the secular one when assessing “the best interests of the child.”25 As we elaborate further below, Rabinovitch is right to criticize the monopoly and primacy granted to Orthodox Judaism in matters of family law in Israel. However, there is a lack of empirical research on the extent to which civil courts actually favor religious parents over secular ones. One or two cases are insufficient to establish a pattern of law in action. Systematic publication of court decisions would enable the empirical examination of this question and allow for evidence-based claims about family law in Israel. Until then, we are forced to be much more modest in describing the field, even when referring to its civil part, let alone its religious one. Reading the chapter, Rabinovitch appears to reinforce a common perception that religious courts systematically disadvantage women, particularly when compared to their civil counterparts.26 When it comes to the Rabbinical courts, and as Rabinovitch demonstrates throughout the book, this common perception stems from the inherently patriarchal nature of Jewish family law. Paramount examples include divorce laws, which result in women remaining agunut (chained to their marriage due to a husband’s disappearance)27 and mesoravot get (women whose husbands refuse to grant them a divorce)28; the all-male composition of the Rabbinical tribunals29; and discriminatory evidence law30; and inheritance law.31 Rabinovitch also relates to Sharia law and the courts’ discrimination against women when he uses a powerful literary illustration, citing Sayed Kashua’s novel Second Person Singular. The citation vividly conveys the deep power asymmetries between men and women before the Sharia court, to the point where the wife character might “never see her kids again,”32 for example, if she committed adultery.33 Other patriarchal elements in Sharia law include, for example, the tolerance of polygamy,34 the one-sided divorce initiated by the husband,35 and the absence of post-divorce spousal maintenance,36 combined with an unequal property division due to the custom of patrilocality.37 Together, these and other elements present a compelling critique of religious adjudication, at least when it comes to Judaism and Islam, as a system that privileges male authority and undermines women’s agency. Rabinovitch’s analysis engages with the broader scholarly debate on multiculturalism and gender, famously framed by Susan Moller Okin’s provocative question: “Is multiculturalism bad for women?”.38 In her canonical 1997 article, Okin argued that patriarchal and anti-feminist cultural and religious practices should not be protected under the banner of multicultural tolerance, and ought to be eradicated. records.title: Dolke, pokaler og magiske søer i Nuristan
records.norm_title: dolke pokaler og magiske soer i nuristan
records.abstract: SILVER, GOLD AND IRON Concerning Katara, Urei, and the Magic Lakes of Nuristan In 1965 Lennart Edelberg published an article entitled Nuristanske Sølvpokaler (KUML 1965, pp. 153-201). The present article is intended to supplement Edelberg's findings on this and related subjects by offering some of the results of fieldwork carried out in Waigal Valley, Nuristan (1). The idea for this paper has been generated by the fact that to the people who live in Waigal valley a silver cup is much more than just something to drink wine out of; a dagger is much more than just a weapon, and certain lakes are much more than just bodies of water. It was in an effort to understand the relationship between certain products of indigenous technology and cultural values that I began, in 1966, to investigate attitudes toward some elements in the Nuristani environment: viz., daggers, silver cups and lakes.Waigal Valley is one of four major drainage areas in Nuristan on the southern slopes of the Hindu Kush in northeast Afghanistan. The other main valley systems are the Bashgal/Nechingal; the Parun/Pech (including Kantiwo) and the Ramgal/Kulum/Titin-Nakara areas to the west Waigal Valley contains nine or ten (2) somewhat widely separated permanent settlements. The smallest village, Want, consists of 6 homesteads; the largest, the combined villages of Waramdesh and Berimdesh (usually called Waigal), approximately 500 houses. The total population of the valley may be 10-12 thousand. The Waigal River flows from north to south and the main valley is some 30 kms. long. The people refer to themselves collectively (and their territory) as the Kalashum.The Waigali-speaking peoples are farmers and herdsmen; the women cultivate millet, maize, barley and wheat on irrigated hill-terraces. The men are responsible for herding the goats, cattle and sheep on a succession of summer pastures where they make butter and cheese. In winter, when snowfalls are often heavy, all livestock are kept in stables near the villages.There is no motor road in the valley, nor is it possible to travel from one village to the next with horses, mules, or donkeys. The villages are connected with each other and with the outside world only by foot trails. Each extended family is economically self-sufficient; there are no markets or organized systems of exchange in the valley. Afghan currency is little used; the standard of value is the goat, though the price of land and houses is usually given in terms of a number of cows.Approximately 90 % of the population of Waigal Valley are atrozan, i.e., they form a free land-owning and livestock-herding class, and each member, by virtue of birth, belongs to a named patri-lineage. These lineages are fixed residential groups and are not dispersed. Marriage is patrilocal. Those lineages the members of which trace descent from a common ancestor form a clan. There are usually two or more clans in a village.The remaining 10 % of the population are either referred to as bari-sewala by Kalashum people, or sometimes, brozan. They are craftsmen and they form a separate, socially and politically disadvantaged minority class in Kalashum society. There is a marriage prohibition between atrozan and brozan. It is said that a bari or sewala may not pass beyond the first pair of columns in an atrozan house; customarily they do not eat together, nor do bari-sewala have any grazing rights. In general they do not own goats, nor do they have an effective voice in village affairs. They form a clearly-defined class, distinguished in everyday life by their traditional occupations. Further, there is a clear distinction, based upon birth, and to some extent, occupation, between bari and sewala. In general bari are skilled craftsmen, while sewala are relatively unskilled. The bari are carpenters and wood-carvers, smiths and jewellers; their wives are weavers. The sewala are potters, basket-makers, leather-workers and porters and are of lower status than bari. The free land-owning, livestock-herding atrozan do not engage in any of these activities. In short, the bari-sewala produce all the material culture of Nuristan.The skills of the bari smith were perhaps best expressed in the production of two highly esteemed objects: the warrior's dagger (katara), and the silver wine cups (urei). I say were because it seems that bari smiths have not made any wine cups for some three or four generations. Sometimes my informants said that their grandfathers had made urei. The warrior's dagger is still made in the Kalashum village of Zhonchigal but these are so inferior in quality as to merely echo the fine work of earlier generations. The best katara made today are turned out by Afghan smiths in the Kabul bazaar. Some are sold to tourists; others find their way to Nuristan.KATARARasically, there are two main types of katara (Fig. 1 and Fig. 2). Only the second type - and a variation of that - is made today. The type shown in Fig. 1 (Type I) is characterized by the fact that its wide-spreading pommel is not only equal in breadth to the quillons, but is formed of two separate components. This type may have its origin in Parun Valley, as Lennart Edelberg once suggested to me, but at present we do not know, as the problem has yet to be investigated in the field. The photograph taken by B.E.M. Gurdon in Chitral in the 1890's (Fig. 3) shows a group of warriors some of whom are carrying type I while others carry type II. This evidence suggests that both types were commonly in use at that time, though today type I is more rare than type II (3). The variation of type II shown in Fig. 4 is that produced today in Zhönchigal and Kabul.What may be described as a third type of katara (Fig. 5) was unearthed in Ameshdesh on the first of September 1969 by women who were cleaning out an irrigation channel. I happened to be present and purchased it from them. A year later, in September 1970, in Nisheigrom, bari Din Mohammed showed me the hilt of a dagger which he had found some years before 'in the mountains' (Fig. 6). He was of the opinion that it was from an ancient Kafir katara - what he called a cima-musti. My own view is that it is more likely to have originated in India (cf. Fig. 7). It could have been obtained via the bazaars in Chitral or Peshawar or it might have been acquired in the course of a trans-border raid. It does, however, seem that the katara shown in Fig. 5 may represent an intermediate type between those known to be of Indian origin (Fig. 7) and the 19th century katara of Nuristan (Figs. 1 & 2). In passing it is also interesting to note the similarity in style between the katara in Fig. 4 and the Jamdhar Katari of Nepal (Fig. 8).We know from Robertson's account (1896) that the katara was a prized possession of every warrior. Even today most men carry one on their belt; a youth is impatient for the day when he can own one, for it is the mark of a man. It is not surprising therefore to find certain old stories or myths connected with these daggers. All the Kalashum stories concerning blacksmiths with which I am familiar invariably make reference to the Gawari-Kawarnä people. According to legend they lived 'between Ningalam and Chagha Serai' (in the lower Pech Valley). This was in the distant past. They were a community of super craftsmen."Gawar is in the mountains above Barkandi. In the old days if a man wanted a fine katara he would go to a certain place near Gawar. On a special stone he would put thirty or forty rupees and then he would leave that place. Two or three days later he would return and there on the stone would be the katara. records.abstract: “New Books across the Disciplines” is a bibliographic resource that facilitates a cross-disciplinary survey of recent publications. Its scope ranges from late antiquity through the seventeenth century. Coverage is comprehensive for the majority of North American and British publishers. Other European titles are included whenever received. Books are classified under variable topical headings and listed alphabetically by author's name. Entries include complete bibliographical data and annotations, including availability in hardcover, paperback, or ebook (OA is indicated for open access ebooks). For paperback reprint editions, original publication dates are given in parentheses. With some exceptions, books appearing here have been published within the previous two years. Many will be presented here before they are ordered and shelved by libraries. Thanks go to David Aers and Sarah Beckwith for their collegial editorial contribution.The topics for this issue include: Biographical studiesJewish studiesChurch, reform, and devotionThe bodyMedicine and healthManuscripts and printed booksAkkerman, Nadine. records.title: Thirteen Surrealist Provocations: Embodied Sacred Activism (We Shall Overcome)
records.norm_title: thirteen surrealist provocations embodied sacred activism we shall overcome
records.abstract: 13 is the most enigmatic of all numbers, as it is the number of transformation. —Pythagoras The thirteen surrealist provocations explored in this essay guide citizen activists to embody the sacred in their everyday lives.1 Each provocation (strategy, principle, and technique) targets a hegemonic force that individually and collectively we can overcome. Wonder (overcome cultural somnambulism) Interconnectedness (overcome epidemic of individualism/ illusion of separation) Hospitality (overcome entitlement/ownership) Ambiguity (overcome tyranny of certainty) Moral Imagination (overcome habituated obedience/complicity) Diversity (overcome xenophobia and ethnocentrism) Non-linearity (overcome progress-at-all-costs) Improvisation (overcome predetermined rules) Intuition (overcome commodifying hegemonies) Collaboration (overcome centralized hierarchy) Deep inquiry (overcome hubris) Interstitiality (overcome binaries) Unfamiliarity (overcome knowledge as acquisition) Unconstrained by the dogma of empire, the limits of so-called reason, and the barbarism of industrial “civilization,” individuals and communities can practice an animated surrealism—activism rooted in the sacred. I suggest that these strategies reflect Stephen Hawking's message, active throughout interfaith cosmologies: everything we need to know is already within us, just waiting to be realized. Through collaborative eco-aesthetics, surrealism engenders trickster consciousness (that which calls into question cultural institutions of normalcy). It represents a lived commitment to transgress hegemonic boundaries of the tyranny of certainty and erasure of difference. These thirteen surrealist strategies challenge extractive, colonizing hegemonies. To illuminate fertile intersections between art and politics, public and private, mind and body, I offer my analog and digital photographs as instantiations of these surrealist provocations. My intent is not to describe my images or use them to illustrate my points, but rather to imagine an exegetical dialogue—a call-and-response—with the text in relation to our daily lives. This Talmudic tactic is central to my surrealist invocation to embody sacred activism. Rather than religion as a prescribed dogma embedded in modernity's insistent homogeneity, sacred activism is a co-evolving collection of dynamic, bio-synergistic individual and collective experiences. Imbibing ancient earth-based technologies such as playing with the sensual corporeality of the human body's relationship to our natural world, respecting objects as subjects, animating plant medicine (familial folk medical systems linked to spiritual pharmacopeias), and redefining waste (echoed in the First Law of Thermodynamics—nothing is created or destroyed, only transformed), sacred activism re-envisions the impossible.2 Following each provocation is a Ladino (Judeo-Spanish) proverb. I invite the reader to enter the fluidity of Ladino consciousness: a dialogue that plays between the personal and political, and veers along the perforated edges of religion, science, politics, ethics, and storytelling. Ladino (the language of my Sephardic maternal and paternal family) is an ultimate polyvocality, a language of cooperation, a hybrid of ancient Spanish, Hebrew, Arabic, and others—depending on where Sephardim fled during expulsions beginning in the fourteenth century.3 Ladino enervates the dialectic between indigenous science and mysticism: observation, intuition, storytelling, and all emanating from the domestic. When we inhabit spiritual intelligence through the thirteen surrealist provocations explored in this essay, the sacred transforms business-as-usual into a continuum of individual-collective awe and wonder. This is sacred activism in action. white stability, a feature of white modernity, the idea that we are isolated, independent selves […] a spatial, temporal arrangement of bodies designed to produce the isolated individual. Whiteness is not white people. Whiteness is the arrangement of bodies in a power structure. It captured white people as much as it captured everyone else. This white modernity is the division of bodies […] what it does not allow us to see is how our bodies are co-terminus with each other, how we are constantly thinking along with microbes and furniture and ancestrality […] that we don't live in a single timeline that proceeds from past to present to future. […] White modernity flattens the world to make it convenient for isolated bodies to walk and then it tells us that we are all alone. (Akómoláfé 2023) Normative nation-state infrastructures violently monitor and eliminate diversity. Centralized power of state-sanctioned violence implies one-truth ideologies, dichotomous “solutions,” and extractive economies. In contrast with pre-ordained rationality based in homogeneous thinking and acting, a nonlinear, nonhierarchical, intuitive, dream-generating economy is rooted in collective, creative risk-taking. It embraces the magical and the mystical. In 1930, when Surrealism was enjoying a peak of public popularity, Einstein wrote: “The most beautiful emotion we can experience is the mysterious.” Reflecting ancient and Indigenous community-based interrelationships that violate sacrosanct “civilized” norms, oikos (the Greek for home and the root of economy and ecology) embodies cultural knowledge, hearth-based spirituality in flux (Figure 1). Our goal should be to live life in radical amazement. […] Get up in the morning and look at the world in a way that takes nothing for granted. —Abraham Joshua Heschel I began photographing in the forests of Westchester County, New York, where I found tree trunks filled with cicada exoskeletons. As if crawling into and emerging from my models' orifices, these symbols of metamorphosis were combined with museum-entombed “exotic” insects, found bats' heads, glass laboratory vials, latex gloves, preserved pigs' ears, mold-encrusted gourds, my fingernail clippings, bird claws and skulls, rusted metal, multiple mirrors/ reflective surfaces, disemboweled roadkill. Here flesh is neither victim nor perpetrator, parasite nor host—yet all of these. I play with objects-as-subjects—my photography props—not as utilitarian objects, but as interrelational subjects—a kinship commons founded on shared ontologies of continuity. Like the trickster who breaks down socially constructed capitalist boundaries between the animate and supposedly inanimate, we recognize the vitality, the value, of every object.5 Following the urgings of Elizabeth Grosz in the context of body awareness and community (Grosz 1995), I co-implicate my photographic props to create new amalgamated social bodies, animations as emanations. Through word and image, stillness, and movement, my intention is to disrupt the distinction between interior and exterior, psychological and physical, and private and public experiences. My eco-surrealist images focus on unmasking industrial society's fossil-fuel addictions while transforming convenience-culture consciousness. My photographic performers (including myself) simultaneously splay our bodies like a trace of memory as we compress ourselves into the present. The quotidian in relation to the sensual spectacle sets up a ritualistic narrative—the collision of strewn bodies and space is simultaneously purposeful and haphazard. I orient my photographic subject objects to elicit deep attention to what already exists—an attunement to our intimacies with the more-than-human world. As an antidote to pervasive fatalistic climate-crisis data, l highlight how we can learn from local ecosystems while embodying beauty to co-create symbiotic communities. By blurring the distinction between the synthetic and the natural, l offer visual narratives that catalyze collective action. Both biomimicry (lessons from nature) and ancient technologies (many of which are still in productive use in the twenty-first century) can be reanimated as lessons for our modern crises. Habituated obedience to fear-based societal norms and behavioral engineering maintained through operational mechanisms of the rational—abdicating our capacity to think, to imagine, and to dream … to wonder. In sharp contrast with biocidal, nation-state thinking, decolonizing socio-spiritual practices throughout Indigenous cosmologies (including Semitic and Levantine-Arabic peoples) echoes a consciousness of wonder and symbiosis—an embodied interrelationality rooted in collective, creative problem-solving. “The language of the Torah is both open ended and compressed in the way dreams are, leaving it open to interpretation and resisting finality” (Eva Lipman, personal conversation 2023). This “unitive, relational theology” (Natan Margalit, personal conversation 2023) represents Judaism's capacity to evolve and adapt. Judaism can be framed as an explicitly surrealist religion: Jewish faith is performed, not believed (Rushkoff 2003, 96). Reminiscent of Heisenberg's “unsharpness” principle, I am the parabolic wandering Jew. My eternal sense of wondering fully inhabits my eternal sense of wandering. Friedrich Ulfers describes this quantum-physics approach to living as one in which we never stop being amazed (Ulfers 2008). Similarly, Wolfgang Schirmacher's elaboration of life techniques insists on claiming our capacity to be in awe (Figure 2). Ladino proverb: Avlar kero, i no puedo, mi korazon sospira (I want to speak, I can't, my heart sighs) If I want to realize totality in my consciousness, I have to relate myself to an immense, ludicrous and painful convulsion of all of humanity. —Georges Bataille, 1985 On Nietzsche Relationality/interconnectivity elicits a different syntax of intimacy, of kinship translations not based in the industrialized Eurometrics that attempt to repeat our hegemonic past, erase our differences, and strip us of our complexities. As with my photographic work, Eva Hesse's 1970s sculptures are material manifestations of Verhängnis, Nietzsche's world of interconnectedness—the collaborative space of hospitality that embraces the ger (Hebrew for stranger), the “unbearable limit between inside and outside, ego and other” (Kristeva 1982, 140). Surrealism as a guide to the sacred reconfigures how society shapes our concept of what is socially acceptable. Conformity creates the illusion of order based on control and homogeneity. Overcoming this sanitized epidemic of individualism, conscious, creative disorder rearranges norms, opening possibilities for co-existing and learning from each other. Because what is outside the familiar is often positioned as deviant by mainstream infrastructures, we must spark courage to embrace our symbiotic differences.
