records.title: Chiang Mai 2015
records.norm_title: chiang mai 2015
records.venue: Gastronomica The Journal of Food and Culture
records.abstract: We landed in Chiang Mai. Nick stood up from his Thai-Airways signature-purple-clad seat, turned his cell phone back on, and announced: “Weird, my phone gives ‘smoke’ as the weather here.” It took ten years to decant, but I now know this comment was a fork in the road, the first crumb leading me, whether I wanted it or not, down a new, meandering trail in the woods. No gingerbread house at the end. The trail is the destination. A trail of enjoyable, forgettable, and unpleasant tastes. A trail of illness.The weather app should have been our first clue that something was awry. As soon as we stepped off the plane, the smell of burning wood engulfed us. It was March 2015, before North Americans became all too familiar with the hazy skies and sullied air caused by massive forest fires (fig. 1). It was late so we went straight to the hotel.My parents met us at breakfast the morning after our arrival. They had flown in separately from Paris and arrived in the middle of the night. Nick and I flew from Toronto first to Singapore and then to Chiang Mai via Bangkok. He was attending a neuropsychiatry conference in Singapore in early March, and I was to return there to participate in a food studies symposium at the end of the month. The timing (and funding) justified a month-long trip, and we decided to visit Thailand between our Singapore events to celebrate our March 15 and 17 birthdays. My parents wanted some warmth in the middle of winter. Nick and I had traveled well with them before and knew their being with us would cover some of our costs. We decided to meet up with them for a couple of weeks. They had had a great time in Vietnam a year earlier, so we picked Thailand as our meeting point since none of us had been there. I would be spending my thirty-first birthday with them, the first time in ten years I could celebrate with my family. And the food was bound to be good.By the time we landed in Chiang Mai, Nick and I had already spent a week on the western Thai island of Koh Mak, chosen as not to be overrun by tourists, which was foolish as we soon learned it was “Thai break” in Germany. Koh Mak had fewer tourist sights than other close-by islands but it made up for it by still having a bustling farming sector. We drove our rented moped through pineapple and Hevea plantations, the latter tapped to gather natural rubber. But the beach had to be raked every morning to remove plastic garbage delivered by the waves. The Pad Thais and curries we recognized from restaurants and takeout in various Western cities we had lived in. The main unexpected culinary element was the cooks’ tendency not to add eggs directly to the Pad Thais but to wrap the noodles inside an omelet instead. I was not yet aware that this dish was a fairly new culinary “invention,” brought forth for nationalistic purposes after the country gained its independence (Greeley 2009; Van Esterik 2000). I thus categorized our island Pad Thais as, “wow, real Thai food.” Another Koh Mak culinary highlight was a pizza prepared by American expats, eaten as we sat in the sand awaiting a ferry ride to a close-by secluded beach. In terms of sensory souvenirs, this pizza beat those Nick and I would eat a few years later in Napoli during our honeymoon. We had one other exceptional Thai meal featuring an appetizer in which the sweetness of palm sugar and the salty sourness of fish sauce mixed with herbaceous notes brought forth by the unknown leaves in which I wrapped my shrimps to form a morsel of flavor I had never experienced. I had finally put my tongue on an “authentic” experience—and here come the scare quotes.I should have known better. By 2015, I had graduated with a doctorate in food history and was well versed in the food studies literature. I knew that the search for “authentic” food, especially the food of populations living in areas occupied by colonial Empires for centuries, is loaded with power relationships, exoticisation, and neocolonial desires to “eat the Other” (Heldke 2008; hooks 1992). My own dissertation (and soon-to-be book) was the story of a doomed search for tradition, albeit in a US context (Bégin 2016). And yet, I continued to roam Thai markets and food stalls to find “the real deal.” The curse of the privileged Western foodie. * * *When we arrived at the hotel’s breakfast courtyard, I was surprised my father was not happier to see me. Jet lag, probably. He went to pick up the rental car as we were to depart for a road trip the day after. We planned to drive to the “golden triangle” at the border of Thailand, Laos, and China, to enjoy famously stunning views of terraced rice paddies and absorb the local culture, cuisine included. We leisurely finished our meal, chatting with my mother, and after a while we wondered why my father was taking so long to return. New city, many rickshaws.It was Nick’s birthday. We visited Chiang Mai’s inner-city temples, where my father snapped a photo of Nick and I banging a gong to ring in Nick’s new year. We bought our dinner at the famed night market where street food stalls offered grilled octopus skewers here, a glass noodle salad there, a Pad Thai a bit further down the crowded road. The skills of the vendors grinding the ingredients for mango salad in their large wooden mortar and pestle fascinated me. I breathed in the pungent smell before tasting the best rendition of the dish I’d ever eaten. We had no time to take any of the cooking classes offered in Chiang Mai, but I think my mother and I would have done so during our planned few days back there after our northern trip. We’ll never know if we would have been able to see beyond the staged, playful authenticity the instructors put on for tourists and that anthropologists love to analyze in their articles (a safe way for them to “eat the Other” under the guise of “doing research”?) (Mills 2019; Walter 2017). By the time we drove back to Chiang Mai, we would no longer be looking for genuine food experiences or novelty—we would be searching for sustenance. * * *Before we left, my parents and I poured over the printouts of our hotel reservation confirmations. It would have been useful to have a map larger than a phone screen.“Papa, why did you use Expedia to plan this trip? You never use Expedia. I don’t get our itinerary, it’s all over the place. The dates seem all mixed up.”“It was useful to keep everything in one place.”“Camille, he won’t let me double check it,” my mother chimed in. “He changed everything two days ago.”“You girls don’t understand the logic. I got it all figured out. Trust me.”“OK, but why does it say you cancelled the reservation in this nice-looking hotel to book us in this subpar one? Why did you change it?” I kept asking questions—none of the bookings made sense to me.“Trust me.”We did not yet know that we were right to question him. * * *Off we went in the rental car, driver on the left in Thailand. My father, who had planned all trips for the past twenty-five years, was the only one who knew where we were going. The roads were in good shape. My father, not always an easy man but usually relaxed and self-assured when traveling, alternated between jolly and his moodiest of moods. One moment he showed his happiness at seeing Nick and I in love, and the next he barked at me for not getting into the car fast enough. We were unsure what to make of his strange behavior.The world-renowned views of Northern Thailand? Nowhere to be seen. Smoke, fog, more smoke. Everywhere. We stopped at viewpoints to look at smoke. Instead of the melodious green camaieu we expected, the landscape was a cacophony of grays and browns—a wall of muffled sounds and heavy smoke. Not a single ray of sunshine made it through. The smell retreated at times, and we were still unsure whether this was fog or smoke, but the higher we got, the more the earthy scent of burning trees reached us. We all hoped for better conditions on the way back down to Chiang Mai. No other tourists were in sight.The hotels? The worst. We arrived at our first hotel at night. It was dark but we could make out several wooden bungalows organized around an empty pool. Either we were the only guests or everyone else was already asleep. The manager (or maybe the owner?) showed the four of us to one bungalow with two sleeping areas separated by a too-short pink curtain. The bungalow was made of dark teak wood. Once inside, I was reminded of an alpine cabin. The decoration was sparse: two pink accent pillows, wooden bedside tables with reading lamps. In my memory the only sources of light were the dim circles under and over the lampshades. We were tired from the drive but had enough in us to demand separate bungalows for the price my father had prepaid. The manager reluctantly showed Nick and me to a similar bungalow, though with orange accents rather than pink. * * *We were settling down for the night when I heard the scream from my parents’ bungalow. records.title: LIVING ARRANGEMENT AND HOMEOWNERSHIP IMPACTS ON FERTILITY INTENTION TO ACHIEVE THE SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT GOALS
records.norm_title: living arrangement and homeownership impacts on fertility intention to achieve the sustainable development goals
records.venue: Journal of Environmental Science and Sustainable Development
records.authors: Umi Salamah; Omas Bulan Samosir; Triasih Djutaharta
records.abstract: A reduction in fertility is among the sustainable development goal indicators in Indonesia. This study analyzed the relationship between living arrangements and home ownership with fertility intention in Indonesia. The inferential analysis used in this study is ordinal logistic regression. The data used in this study came from the National Socioeconomic Survey 2017 results. The unit analysis in this study was women aged 15-49 years who were married and not contracepting. The dependent variable in this study was the fertility intention. The independent variables, namely living arrangement and home ownership, and the control variables, namely women's age, women's education, women's working status, parity, husband's education, husband's working status, living area, household income, grandparent's age, grandparent's health status, grandparent's working status, and grandparent's gender. This study was divided into three models. In the first model, women who live with their parents have 1.17 times higher tendency to have high fertility intentions than those with low fertility intentions or do not have fertility intentions than women who do not live with their parents. In the third model, women who live with their parents have 1.11 times higher tendency to have high fertility intentions than those who have low fertility intentions or do not have fertility intentions compared to women who do not live with their parents. The study results show that women who lived with their parents had higher odds of having high fertility intention. Women who lived in homes that were not their own tended to have high fertility intentions. From these results, it is hoped that there will be programs from the government for the elderly family so that the presence of parents or inlaws in the household can improve the quality of children more than the number of children.
